text: 🔥 Ending gas flaring alone could recover up to 2.4 billion cubic feet per day. "Pemex must develop a plan to increase the gas supply with conventional production and avoid burning that resource in oil fields." — Alma América Porres Luna, hydrocarbons expert The committee estimates up to 2,400 MMcf/d from eliminating flaring, plus up to 4,700 MMcf/d from conventional fields in Burgos, Tampico-Misantla, Veracruz and the southeast basins.

🗳️ "There will be a public consultation before any production begins." "An informed consultation, where the people who live nearby can tell us whether they agree or not with this type of exploitation... These are the conclusions. We take them as they come." — Presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo Sheinbaum said IMTA will drill exploratory water wells first: if no salt water is found, the possibility of non-conventional gas extraction "closes." All committee studies will be published on the Secihti and Energy Ministry sites.
banner: "WE TAKE THE CONCLUSIONS AS THEY COME"

text: 💧 No fresh water for fracking: only deep salt water, 75% recycled. "Under no circumstances should fresh water be used... we recommend employing exclusively salt water... and recycling at least 75% of the water used." — José Antonio Hernández Espriú, UNAM Faculty of Engineering A single fracking well needs 50,000-70,000 m³ of water. The committee requires confirming deep salt-water bodies — hydraulically disconnected from freshwater aquifers — before any production.

🚫 Scientists recommend banning fracking in the Tampico-Misantla basin. "By criteria of environmental protection, social impact, biodiversity and demographic density, activities in non-conventional gas fields in the Tampico-Misantla basin should be prohibited." — Ana Paulina Gómora, UNAM Faculty of Engineering The committee said evaluation may continue only in two basins: Sabinas-Burro-Picachos (Coahuila, Nuevo León) and Burgos (northeast Tamaulipas). Sheinbaum accepted the recommendation on the spot.

🔬 54 scientists, one consensus: public decisions must rest on evidence. "Public decisions must be sustained by evidence, protect the environment and generate greater benefit for the people of Mexico." — Rosaura Ruiz, Science Secretary The Scientific Committee on non-conventional gas — 54 experts from UNAM, IMP, IMTA and independent institutions — delivered its first conclusions after nearly three months of work. Everything was decided by consensus.

⚡ Mexico imports 75% of the natural gas it consumes — all of it from the US. "The high dependence Mexico has on these imports compromises our sovereignty and energy security." — Alma América Porres Luna, hydrocarbons expert, Scientific Committee Mexico consumes 9.1 billion cubic feet of gas per day; 58% goes to electricity. Imports were 21% of demand in 2010 — today 75%, and 93% of imported gas comes from US shale plays.

🔥🇲🇽 <u>CDMX DECLARES WAR ON PROPERTY-THEFT NETWORKS</u>

Clara Brugada's government launched a unified plan against real-estate dispossession: stolen properties secured within 15 days, trials opened in 30, twenty specialized courts, police responding in under three minutes, and a new Defensoría Jurídica offering free legal aid — with lawyers posted in the Zócalo every week. "In Mexico City there will be no room for dispossession networks," Brugada said; prosecutor Bertha Alcalde added the crime now carries up to 22 years in prison.
banner: CDMX: 15 DAYS TO RECOVER STOLEN HOMES

🚨🇲🇽 <u>WASHINGTON PUTS A $102 MILLION PRICE TAG ON THE CJNG</u>

The US State Department raised the bounty on CJNG boss Juan Carlos "El Pelón" Valencia to $25 million and is offering up to $102 million total for eight top figures of the cartel. Since June 2025, Washington has cancelled 93 visas of cartel relatives and associates — 65 of them in this round — while the DOJ filed new charges against five named operatives. All under the "foreign terrorist organization" label Mexico rejects as an intervention pretext.
banner: US PUTS $102M BOUNTY ON CJNG LEADERS

text:
🔥🇲🇽 <u>THE OPPOSITION'S SCRIPT: SUBORDINATION SOLD AS MODERNITY</u>

In Contralínea, philosopher Fernando Buen Abad Domínguez breaks down how Mexico's right-wing alliance works long before any pact is signed: "The plunder begins in the dictionary long before it settles into the institutions." The cognitive war doesn't need to abolish the Constitution — it's enough to make it invisible, repainting dependence as opportunity and sovereignty as backwardness. Mexico's opposition, he argues, doesn't arrive wrapped in foreign flags; it shows up speaking the national language, selling the handover of strategic assets as the price of the future.

🚨🇲🇽 <u>WASHINGTON FREEZES MEXICAN AVOCADO EXPORTS — MEXICO ANSWERS</u>

The US suspended USDA inspections in Michoacán over a vague "security threat" to its personnel, halting shipments from the state that supplies 80% of the avocados Americans eat. Packers were told only fruit received before August 4 can still be processed. Mexico didn't wait: Sheinbaum's government requested an urgent meeting with the USDA, offered Senasica inspectors as replacements, and deployed 1,500 soldiers to the avocado belt. Mexico sells, Washington blocks — and Mexico still fixes it.
